title: Amazon's Zoox Wins US Approval for Paid Rides Without Steering Wheels
excerpt: NHTSA grants first-ever commercial exemption for a purpose-built robotaxi lacking human controls, clearing the way for paid rides in Las Vegas next month.
body:
• Amazon's Zoox has received the first US federal approval allowing a robotaxi without a steering wheel or pedals to charge passengers for rides.
  • NHTSA's exemption permits Zoox to deploy up to 2,500 vehicles per year for two years, with paid service launching in Las Vegas next month.
  • The agency simultaneously announced plans for the first-ever federal safety standards for autonomous driving systems.
  • Zoox must meet strict reporting requirements on crashes and operational anomalies, and NHTSA retains the power to revoke the exemption.

Amazon's autonomous vehicle unit Zoox has won federal approval to begin charging passengers for rides in its steering-wheel-free robotaxis — a first for the US autonomous ride-hailing industry. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced the commercial exemption on Thursday, clearing a regulatory hurdle that has kept purpose-built driverless vehicles from operating as paid services.

The exemption allows Zoox to deploy up to 2,500 of its electric, carriage-style vehicles annually for two years. Paid service will launch first in Las Vegas next month, with additional markets to follow as the company secures state and local approvals. Zoox currently operates free rides in parts of Las Vegas and San Francisco, having carried more than 500,000 passengers during its testing phase.

"Today marks an important milestone for Zoox and the future of autonomous mobility."

— Aicha Evans, CEO, Zoox

What NHTSA Approved — and What It Didn't

The exemption waives federal rules requiring human controls like steering wheels, brake pedals, and mirrors — regulations written decades before self-driving technology existed. NHTSA determined that Zoox's systems meet or exceed the performance requirements of vehicles that comply with those standards.

"We can say pretty clearly that the systems in place on the Zoox exceed the equivalent performance requirements of a compliant vehicle," NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison told Reuters. "But we still want to make sure that the automated driving system will operate appropriately."

The approval is temporary and comes with strings attached. Zoox must file detailed reports on crashes, software anomalies, and instances of vehicles stopping inappropriately on roads. All remote operators must be based in the United States, and the company must publish maps showing where its vehicles operate. NHTSA retains the authority to revoke the exemption.

"We have the ability to pull the exemption if we see major safety issues," Morrison said.

A Broader Regulatory Shift

Alongside the Zoox exemption, NHTSA announced plans to develop the first-ever national regulatory standards for autonomous vehicles. The US has long relied on a patchwork of state and local rules to govern fully driverless cars. The agency is also proposing to eliminate the federal requirement for manual brake pedals in vehicles designed exclusively for autonomous operation — a separate rule change that could benefit companies like Tesla, whose Cybercab concept was designed without pedals or a steering wheel.

Morrison said NHTSA expects to have federal safety standards for automated driving systems in place by the end of the Trump administration. The agency also withdrew a Biden-era proposal for a voluntary national framework for evaluating self-driving vehicles, signaling a shift toward binding standards.

Competitive Landscape Heats Up

The approval comes as the US robotaxi market intensifies. Alphabet's Waymo currently leads in scale, while Tesla has begun offering ride-hailing services in seven US cities. But Zoox has taken a distinct approach: rather than retrofitting conventional cars, the company has built its vehicle from scratch at its California manufacturing facility. The result is a boxy, symmetrical pod with sliding doors, two rows of inward-facing seats, and a top speed of 75 mph.

Zoox is now testing in at least 10 US markets and has an arrangement with Uber for its Las Vegas operations. The company is targeting production capacity of up to 10,000 robotaxis per year as it expands.

Safety Questions Remain

The approval arrives amid ongoing scrutiny of autonomous vehicle safety. Earlier this month, Morrison issued a letter urging AV developers to "immediately focus" on fixing what NHTSA identified as "a clear pattern of driverless AVs interfering with law enforcement and other first responders." Issues including robotaxis driving past stopped school buses, entering construction zones, and freezing at busy intersections have fueled public concern and triggered recalls across the industry.

Zoox itself recently recalled its fleet of 105 autonomous vehicles after discovering they might not detect heavy smoke, particularly during active emergencies. The recall, involving a software update, came shortly after Morrison's safety directive.

For the autonomous vehicle industry, the Zoox exemption represents a proof of concept: purpose-built robotaxis can navigate the US regulatory process and reach commercial deployment. Whether the technology can earn public trust at scale remains the bigger question.
nri_angle: The approval accelerates the US autonomous vehicle market, a sector with significant Indian-origin engineering and leadership talent across Waymo, Tesla, and Amazon's robotics divisions.
